claim: Eukaryotic cell division requires the mitotic spindle, a microtubule (MT)-based structure which accurately aligns and segregates duplicated chromosomes.
source: Eukaryotic cell division requires the mitotic spindle, a microtubule (MT)-based structure which accurately aligns and segregates duplicated chromosomes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the role of the mitotic spindle in cell division.

claim: The dynamics of spindle formation are determined primarily by correctly localising the MT nucleator, γ-Tubulin Ring Complex (γ-TuRC), within the cell.
source: The dynamics of spindle formation are determined primarily by correctly localising the MT nucleator, γ-Tubulin Ring Complex (γ-TuRC), within the cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of γ-TuRC in spindle formation.

claim: Augmin recruits γ-TuRC to pre-existing spindle MTs, amplifying their number, in an essential cellular phenomenon termed 'branching' MT nucleation.
source: A conserved MT-associated protein complex, Augmin, recruits γ-TuRC to pre-existing spindle MTs, amplifying their number, in an essential cellular phenomenon termed 'branching' MT nucleation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Augmin's function in branching MT nucleation.

claim: Endogenous, GFP-tagged Augmin and γ-TuRC can be purified from Drosophila embryos to near homogeneity using a novel one-step affinity technique.
source: Here, we purify endogenous, GFP-tagged Augmin and γ-TuRC from Drosophila embryos to near homogeneity using a novel one-step affinity technique.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated by the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Augmin alone does not affect Tubulin polymerisation dynamics in vitro.
source: We demonstrate that, in vitro, while Augmin alone does not affect Tubulin polymerisation dynamics, it stimulates γ-TuRC-dependent MT nucleation in a cell cycle-dependent manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymerization assay data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Augmin stimulates γ-TuRC-dependent MT nucleation in a cell cycle-dependent manner in vitro.
source: We demonstrate that, in vitro, while Augmin alone does not affect Tubulin polymerisation dynamics, it stimulates γ-TuRC-dependent MT nucleation in a cell cycle-dependent manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymerization assay data comparing mitotic and cycling complexes in Figure 2c.

claim: The MT-Augmin-γ-TuRC-MT junction can be assembled and visualised using light microscopy.
source: We also assemble and visualise the MT-Augmin-γ-TuRC-MT junction using light microscopy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data in Figure 3c-g.

claim: Branching MT nucleation is dependent upon Augmin and γ-TuRC.
source: Branching MT nucleation is dependent upon Augmin and γ-TuRC and generates the bulk of MTs required for both meiotic and mitotic spindle formation (Petry et al., 2011; Sánchez-Huertas and Lüders, 2015; David et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Branching MT nucleation generates the bulk of MTs required for both meiotic and mitotic spindle formation.
source: Branching MT nucleation is dependent upon Augmin and γ-TuRC and generates the bulk of MTs required for both meiotic and mitotic spindle formation (Petry et al., 2011; Sánchez-Huertas and Lüders, 2015; David et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Branching MT nucleation has been visualised in vivo in Drosophila, Xenopus, plants, and humans.
source: and has been visualised in vivo in Drosophila, Xenopus, plants, and humans (Petry et al., 2011; David et al., 2019; Hayward et al., 2014; Ho et al., 2011; Lawo et al., 2009; Goshima et al., 2008; Uehara et al., 2009; Prosser and Pelletier, 2017; Petry et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Understanding and in vitro reconstitution of branching MT nucleation has been hampered by methodological constraints relating to purification of functional protein complexes.
source: However, understanding, and in vitro reconstitution of, this phenomenon has been hampered by methodological constraints relating to purification of functional protein complexes (Hsia et al., 2014; Song et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Augmin is composed of 8 subunits.
source: Augmin is composed of 8 subunits, while the γ-TuRC is a ~ 2 MD protein complex containing multiple copies of at least six proteins, including 14 molecules of γ-Tubulin (Zheng et al., 1995; Moritz et al., 1995; Kollman et al., 2011; Tovey and Conduit, 2018; Oegema et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The γ-TuRC is a ~ 2 MD protein complex containing multiple copies of at least six proteins, including 14 molecules of γ-Tubulin.
source: Augmin is composed of 8 subunits, while the γ-TuRC is a ~ 2 MD protein complex containing multiple copies of at least six proteins, including 14 molecules of γ-Tubulin (Zheng et al., 1995; Moritz et al., 1995; Kollman et al., 2011; Tovey and Conduit, 2018; Oegema et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In vitro studies generally use proteins that have been individually- or co-expressed and purified in heterologous systems.
source: In vitro studies (Oegema et al., 1999) generally use proteins that have been individually- or co-expressed and purified in heterologous systems (Trokter et al., 2012; Schlager et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Folding and post translational modifications crucial to function may not occur in heterologous expression systems.
source: where folding and post translational modifications crucial to function may not occur.
evidence: This is established knowledge about limitations of heterologous expression systems.

claim: Non-specific binding of contaminating proteins and difficulties in releasing purified proteins from affinity matrices are major problems in affinity-based purification methods.
source: Although purification of protein complexes from autogenous cells can be achieved using affinity-based methods, non-specific binding of contaminating proteins and difficulties in releasing purified proteins from affinity matrices are major problems.
evidence: This is established knowledge about limitations of affinity purification methods.

claim: The purification approach is based on biotinylated, amine-reactive thiol- or photo-cleavable linkers, Sulfo-NHS-SS-Biotin and PC-Biotin-NHS.
source: The approach is based on biotinylated, amine-reactive thiol- or photo-cleavable linkers, Sulfo-NHS-SS-Biotin and PC-Biotin-NHS (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the methodology shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Stepwise incubation of the ~12 kD camelid anti-GFP nanobody with cleavable linkers results in covalent linkage.
source: Stepwise incubation of the ~12 kD camelid anti-GFP nanobody, GFP-binding protein, with either of these linkers resulted in covalent linkage
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Incubation of GFP-binding protein-linker conjugates with Streptavidin Agarose matrix leads to stable tri-partite reagents where GFP-binding protein is immobilised but cleavable through the addition of DTT or exposure to UV light.
source: while subsequent incubation with a Streptavidin Agarose matrix led to stable tri-partite reagents – GFP-TRAP-Sulfo beads and GFP-TRAP-PC beads; where GFP-binding protein is immobilised, but cleavable through the addition of DTT or exposure to UV light, respectively (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the methodology and data shown in Figure 1a-c.

claim: Upon brief exposure to 50 mM DTT or UV light, fluorescence of GFP-TRAP beads decreased, concomitant with an increase in the surrounding medium.
source: Individual beads fluoresced with varying intensity and, upon brief exposure to 50 mM DTT or UV light, fluorescence decreased, concomitant with an increase in the surrounding medium (Figure 1b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: >90% of GFP was released from GFP-TRAP-Sulfo beads following cleavage.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed >90% and~60% of GFP was released from GFP-TRAP-Sulfo and GFP-TRAP-PC beads, respectively, following cleavage (Figure 1c; Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Western blot data in Figure 1c.

claim: ~60% of GFP was released from GFP-TRAP-PC beads following cleavage.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed >90% and~60% of GFP was released from GFP-TRAP-Sulfo and GFP-TRAP-PC beads, respectively, following cleavage (Figure 1c; Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Drosophila Augmin can be purified from extracts of early embryos expressing a GFP-tagged variant of the Msd1 subunit.
source: We have previously shown that Drosophila Augmin can be purified from extracts of early embryos expressing a GFP-tagged variant of the Msd1 subunit (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Drosophila embryos have been used to purify the γ-TuRC.
source: Drosophila embryos have also been used to purify the γ-TuRC (Oegema et al., 1999; Moritz et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Branching MT nucleation is essential during mitosis.
source: As branching MT nucleation is essential during mitosis, we used embryos arrested in a metaphase-like state through incubation with the proteasomal inhibitor, MG132 (Chesnel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Both Msd1-GFP and γ-Tubulin-GFP were efficiently immobilised on GFP-TRAP-Sulfo or GFP-TRAP-PC beads.
source: Both Msd1-GFP and γ-Tubulin-GFP were efficiently immobilised on GFP-TRAP-Sulfo or GFP-TRAP-PC beads and western blotting confirmed that, upon cleaving, Msd1-GFP and γ-Tubulin-GFP were concentrated in the eluate, with other subunits of the complexes co-eluting (Figure 1d; Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Western blot data in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Upon cleaving, Msd1-GFP and γ-Tubulin-GFP were concentrated in the eluate, with other subunits of the complexes co-eluting.
source: Both Msd1-GFP and γ-Tubulin-GFP were efficiently immobilised on GFP-TRAP-Sulfo or GFP-TRAP-PC beads and western blotting confirmed that, upon cleaving, Msd1-GFP and γ-Tubulin-GFP were concentrated in the eluate, with other subunits of the complexes co-eluting (Figure 1d; Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Western blot data in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Bands corresponding to each subunit of both Augmin and γ-TuRC were identified at intensities expected for the known stoichiometric relationships between subunits.
source: Bands corresponding to each subunit of both Augmin and γ-TuRC were identified at intensities expected for the known stoichiometric relationships between subunits (Oegema et al., 1999).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SYPRO-ruby stained gel in Figure 1e and supported by citation.

claim: One additional set of low intensity bands was seen in all eluates, at ~45 kD, almost certainly corresponding to yolk proteins.
source: One additional set of low intensity bands was seen in all eluates, at ~45 kD; almost certainly corresponding to yolk proteins - the most abundant proteins in Drosophila early embryos (Barnett et al., 1980).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SYPRO-ruby stained gel in Figure 1e and supported by citation about yolk proteins.

claim: γ-Tubulin did not co-purify with Augmin.
source: Importantly, γ-Tubulin did not co-purify with Augmin, and Dgt3 (a subunit of the Augmin complex) did not co-purify with γ-TuRC (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Western blot data in Figure 1d.

claim: Dgt3 (a subunit of the Augmin complex) did not co-purify with γ-TuRC.
source: Importantly, γ-Tubulin did not co-purify with Augmin, and Dgt3 (a subunit of the Augmin complex) did not co-purify with γ-TuRC (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Western blot data in Figure 1d.

claim: Msd1-GFP sedimented as expected for Augmin-GFP (~360 kD) in sucrose gradient analysis.
source: Moreover, sucrose gradient analysis undertaken on purified mitotic complexes determined that Msd1-GFP sedimented as expected for Augmin-GFP (~360 kD) and that γ-Tubulin-GFP sedimented in two populations – one consistent with γ-Tubulin-GFP alone and one consistent with incorporation into the γ-TuRC (2MD) (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sucrose gradient fractionation data in Figure 1f.

claim: γ-Tubulin-GFP sedimented in two populations – one consistent with γ-Tubulin-GFP alone and one consistent with incorporation into the γ-TuRC (2MD).
source: Moreover, sucrose gradient analysis undertaken on purified mitotic complexes determined that Msd1-GFP sedimented as expected for Augmin-GFP (~360 kD) and that γ-Tubulin-GFP sedimented in two populations – one consistent with γ-Tubulin-GFP alone and one consistent with incorporation into the γ-TuRC (2MD) (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sucrose gradient fractionation data in Figure 1f.

claim: Augmin and γ-TuRC do not co-fractionate in sucrose gradients.
source: Neither complex co-fractionated, again strongly suggesting that Augmin and γ-TuRC are purified independently of one another, or other cellular activities.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sucrose gradient fractionation data in Figure 1f.

claim: Both γ-TuRC and Augmin bind MTs in co-sedimentation assays.
source: Both γ-TuRC and Augmin bind MTs in co-sedimentation assays (Hughes et al., 2008; Wainman et al., 2009; Goshima et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Both Msd1-GFP and γ-Tubulin-GFP co-sedimented with MTs in the presence of taxol.
source: As expected, both Msd1-GFP and γ-Tubulin-GFP co-sedimented with MTs, demonstrating purified Augmin and γ-TuRC maintain at least some of their cellular properties.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MT co-sedimentation assay data in Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Purified Augmin and γ-TuRC maintain at least some of their cellular properties.
source: As expected, both Msd1-GFP and γ-Tubulin-GFP co-sedimented with MTs, demonstrating purified Augmin and γ-TuRC maintain at least some of their cellular properties.
evidence: This is inferred from the MT co-sedimentation assay results.

claim: Addition of purified γ-TuRC-GFP stimulated MT nucleation, reducing the x50 from 31.5 mins to 16.5 mins.
source: Addition of purified γ-TuRC-GFP stimulated MT nucleation, causing a shift in the polymerisation curve and a reduction in the x50 to 16.5 mins (± 1.2 min) (Figure 2a,b), confirming its functionality.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymerization assay data in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Addition of purified Augmin-GFP had no significant effect on the shape of the polymerisation curve or the x50.
source: In contrast, addition of purified Augmin-GFP had no significant effect on the shape of the polymerisation curve or the x50 (32.5 mins (± 1.5 min) (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymerization assay data in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Although Augmin-GFP binds MTs it does not, in isolation, change MT nucleation/polymerisation dynamics.
source: Therefore, although Augmin-GFP binds MTs it does not, in isolation, change MT nucleation/polymerisation dynamics.
evidence: This is inferred from the polymerization assay results showing no effect of Augmin alone.

claim: Addition of Augmin-GFP dramatically enhanced γ-TuRC-dependent nucleation of MTs, further reducing the x50 to 9.5 min.
source: However, addition of Augmin-GFP dramatically enhanced γ-TuRC-dependent nucleation of MTs, further reducing the x50 to 9.5 min (± 0.45 min) (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymerization assay data in Figure 2a,b.

claim: The effect of Augmin on γ-TuRC-dependent MT nucleation was specific for the physical interaction between Augmin and γ-TuRC.
source: This effect was specific for the physical interaction between Augmin and γ-TuRC, as addition of bacterially expressed and purified truncated Augmin subunits, Dgt3, Dgt5 and Dgt6, which we previously demonstrated interact directly with γ-TuRC (Chen et al., 2017), resulted in nucleation/polymerisation curves indistinguishable to γ-TuRC alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymerization assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and supported by citation.

claim: Truncated Augmin subunits Dgt3, Dgt5 and Dgt6 interact directly with γ-TuRC.
source: as addition of bacterially expressed and purified truncated Augmin subunits, Dgt3, Dgt5 and Dgt6, which we previously demonstrated interact directly with γ-TuRC (Chen et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Purified Augmin augments γ-TuRC-dependent MT nucleation in vitro.
source: Thus, purified Augmin does, indeed, augment γ-TuRC-dependent MT nucleation in vitro.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the polymerization assay data.

claim: The augmenting phenomenon was dependent on whether the complexes were isolated from mitotically arrested (MG132) or untreated, mainly interphase (cycling) embryos.
source: Importantly, this phenomenon was dependent on whether the complexes were isolated from mitotically arrested (MG132) or untreated, mainly interphase (cycling) embryos.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymerization assay data in Figure 2c.

claim: γ-TuRC purified from cycling embryos was a less efficient nucleator than its mitotic counterpart.
source: γ-TuRC purified from cycling embryos was a less efficient nucleator than its mitotic counterpart (Figure 2c; Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymerization assay data in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cycling Augmin, like mitotic Augmin, showed no independent activity on MT nucleation.
source: while cycling Augmin, like mitotic Augmin, showed no independent activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymerization assay data in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Either mitotic γ-TuRC and cycling Augmin or cycling γ-TuRC and mitotic Augmin were able to enhance MT nucleation to the same extent as both mitotic complexes.
source: However, when incubated together, either mitotic γ-TuRC and cycling Augmin or cycling γ-TuRC and mitotic Augmin were able to enhance MT nucleation to the same extent as both mitotic complexes (Figure 2c; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymerization assay data in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cell cycle dependent changes in protein function are determined mostly by post-translational modifications (PTMs).
source: As cell cycle dependent changes in protein function are determined mostly by post-translational modifications (PTMs), this observation suggests that PTMs of either Augmin or γ-Tubulin are crucial in vivo.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle regulation.

claim: PTMs of either Augmin or γ-Tubulin are crucial in vivo for branching MT nucleation.
source: As cell cycle dependent changes in protein function are determined mostly by post-translational modifications (PTMs), this observation suggests that PTMs of either Augmin or γ-Tubulin are crucial in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that either mitotic Augmin or mitotic γ-TuRC is sufficient for enhanced nucleation.

claim: Samples containing purified Augmin showed only very few, short MTs per field of view at t = 15 min.
source: Control samples, or those containing purified Augmin, showed only very few, short MTs per field of view while, as expected, γ-TuRC-containing samples possessed many individual MTs (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data in Figure 3a.

claim: γ-TuRC-containing samples possessed many individual MTs at t = 15 min.
source: Control samples, or those containing purified Augmin, showed only very few, short MTs per field of view while, as expected, γ-TuRC-containing samples possessed many individual MTs (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data in Figure 3a.

claim: Samples incubated simultaneously with γ-TuRC and Augmin showed extensive MT branching, bundling and nesting, rather than individual MTs.
source: In contrast, samples incubated simultaneously with γ-TuRC and Augmin showed extensive MT branching, bundling and nesting, rather than individual MTs (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data in Figure 3a.

claim: Purified mitotic Augmin was able to recruit purified γ-TuRC to MTs in vitro, co-localising along the length of MTs in distinct punctae.
source: Moreover, consistent with the observation that, in vivo, Augmin is required for γ-Tubulin localisation to the mitotic spindle, purified mitotic Augmin was able to recruit purified γ-TuRC to MTs in vitro, co-localising along the length of MTs in distinct punctae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: In vivo, Augmin is required for γ-Tubulin localisation to the mitotic spindle.
source: Moreover, consistent with the observation that, in vivo, Augmin is required for γ-Tubulin localisation to the mitotic spindle
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Within 1 min of the simultaneous addition of Augmin and γ-TuRC, MT nucleation and putative branching were observed.
source: Even within 1 min of the simultaneous addition of Augmin and γ-TuRC, MT nucleation and putative branching were observed, though background fluorescence of soluble tubulin was high (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data in Figure 3b.

claim: The mean length of MTs was significantly greater after 5 min than after 2 min (4.01 μm versus 3.24 μm).
source: Samples taken at t = 2 and t = 5 min showed similar numbers of MTs to each other, per field of view, though the mean length of MTs, and proportion of MTs with branches, were significantly greater after 5 min, than after 2 min (4.01 μm versus 3.24 μm and 34% versus 24%, respectively) (Figure 3b; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data and quantification in Figure 3b and Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: The proportion of MTs with branches was significantly greater after 5 min than after 2 min (34% versus 24%).
source: Samples taken at t = 2 and t = 5 min showed similar numbers of MTs to each other, per field of view, though the mean length of MTs, and proportion of MTs with branches, were significantly greater after 5 min, than after 2 min (4.01 μm versus 3.24 μm and 34% versus 24%, respectively) (Figure 3b; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data and quantification in Figure 3b and Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: MT nucleation from purified γ-TuRCs reaches maximal activity within the first few minutes of the assay.
source: This suggests that MT nucleation from purified γ-TuRCs reaches maximal activity within the first few minutes of the assay.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MT numbers are similar at 2 and 5 minutes.

claim: The estimated number of γ-TuRCs per coverslip (6.0 x 10^6) was 2-3 times less than the mean number of MTs per coverslip (1.7 x 10^7).
source: Moreover, the estimated number of γ-TuRCs per coverslip (6.0 x 106) was 2-3 times less than the mean number of MTs per coverslip (1.7 x 107) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data as described in Materials and methods.

claim: A single γ-TuRC may be able to nucleate multiple MTs at a rate of >1 MT/min.
source: These calculations suggest ﻿﻿either (i) that our approximations of γ-TuRC molarity are out by a factor of 2-3, (ii) that the MTs counted include a proportion that have been nucleated by a γ-TuRC and subsequently broken or (iii) that a single γ-TuRC is able to nucleate multiple MTs at a rate of >1 MT/min, perhaps by nucleation and subsequent release.
evidence: This is one of three possible explanations inferred from the calculation that there are more MTs than γ-TuRCs.

claim: 55% of γ-TuRC-containing RhodMTs terminated precisely at an Augmin-containing 488MT.
source: However, when RhodMTs incubated with γ-TuRC were added together with 488MTs incubated with Augmin, 55% of γ-TuRC-containing RhodMTs terminated precisely at an Augmin-containing 488MT (Figure 3c–e; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data and quantification in Figure 3c-e and Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: The polarity and angles of the RhodMTs branches in relation to the 'mother' 488MTs varied far more widely than seen in vivo.
source: Although the polarity and angles of the RhodMTs branches in relation to the 'mother' 488MTs varied far more widely than seen in vivo, presumably due to how the MTs settled on the coverslip during preparation, we found a bias in the angle, similar to that seen in living Drosophila (Verma and Maresca, 2019) (Figure 3e; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the angle distribution data in Figure 3e and Figure 3—source data 1, and compared to in vivo data by citation.

claim: There is a bias in the branch angle similar to that seen in living Drosophila.
source: Although the polarity and angles of the RhodMTs branches in relation to the 'mother' 488MTs varied far more widely than seen in vivo, presumably due to how the MTs settled on the coverslip during preparation, we found a bias in the angle, similar to that seen in living Drosophila (Verma and Maresca, 2019) (Figure 3e; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the angle distribution data in Figure 3e and Figure 3—source data 1, and supported by citation.

claim: The polarity of the interaction between γ-TuRC-RhodMTs and Augmin-488MTs was specific; with only the minus ends of γ-TuRC-RhodMTs precisely terminating at the Augmin-488MTs lateral surfaces.
source: As expected, the polarity of the interaction between γ-TuRC-RhodMTs and Augmin-488MTs was specific; with only the minus ends of γ-TuRC-RhodMTs precisely terminating at the Augmin-488MTs lateral surfaces (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data using GMPCPP seeds in Figure 3g.

claim: The percentage of γ-TuRC-RhodMTs generating branches increased to 64% when GMPCPP seeds were used.
source: Moreover, as predicted, the percentage of γ-TuRC-RhodMTs generating branches further increased to 64% (Figure 3e; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantification data in Figure 3e and Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: The formation of junctions on Augmin-containing 488MTs was length independent – branches were equally distributed at the very distal MT tips, throughout their length and on the GMPCPP seed itself.
source: Finally, we found that the formation of junctions on Augmin-containing 488MTs was length independent – branches were equally distributed at the very distal MT tips, throughout their length and on the GMPCPP seed itself (Figure 3g,h; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data and correlation analysis in Figure 3g,h and Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: Augmin directly recruits γ-TuRC to MTs.
source: It demonstrates conclusively that Augmin directly recruits γ-TuRC to MTs and that these two protein complexes are sufficient for robust and efficient branching MT nucleation.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the reconstitution experiments.

claim: Augmin and γ-TuRC are sufficient for robust and efficient branching MT nucleation.
source: It demonstrates conclusively that Augmin directly recruits γ-TuRC to MTs and that these two protein complexes are sufficient for robust and efficient branching MT nucleation.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the reconstitution experiments.

claim: 65% of the mitotic γ-TuRCs are competent to bind MT minus ends and Augmin.
source: Although our calculations suggest that 65% of the mitotic γ-TuRCs are competent to bind MT minus ends and Augmin, and that they are able to nucleate at a rate of >1 MT/min, we expect that, in vivo, other proteins further enhance these γ-TuRC activities.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data showing 64% of γ-TuRC-RhodMTs forming branches.

claim: Purified γ-TuRCs are able to nucleate at a rate of >1 MT/min.
source: Although our calculations suggest that 65% of the mitotic γ-TuRCs are competent to bind MT minus ends and Augmin, and that they are able to nucleate at a rate of >1 MT/min, we expect that, in vivo, other proteins further enhance these γ-TuRC activities.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data on MT numbers and γ-TuRC amounts.

claim: In vivo, other proteins further enhance γ-TuRC activities.
source: Although our calculations suggest that 65% of the mitotic γ-TuRCs are competent to bind MT minus ends and Augmin, and that they are able to nucleate at a rate of >1 MT/min, we expect that, in vivo, other proteins further enhance these γ-TuRC activities.
evidence: This is speculation based on the authors' expectations.

claim: TPX2 has a clear role in stimulating Augmin-dependent branched MT nucleation in Xenopus meiotic extracts.
source: For example, a clear role has been reported for the MT associated protein, TPX2, in stimulating Augmin-dependent branched MT nucleation in Xenopus meiotic extracts (Petry et al., 2013; Thawani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Drosophila TPX2 has been shown to be dispensible for branching MT nucleation in vivo.
source: However, in support of our conclusions, Drosophila TPX2 has recently been shown to be dispensible for the phenomenon in vivo (Verma and Maresca, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent literature.

claim: In some cells, Augmin might recruit pre-existing γ-TuRC-containing MTs, nucleated elsewhere in the cell, anchoring them to specific sites and increasing local MT density.
source: Our experiments also highlight the intriguing possibility that, in some cells, Augmin might recruit pre-existing γ-TuRC-containing MTs, nucleated elsewhere in the cell, anchoring them to specific sites and increasing local MT density.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The methodologies provide a route to defining the molecular detail of MT branching at the ultrastructural level.
source: The generation of stable MT-Augmin-γ-TuRC-MT junctions using the methodologies pioneered here also provide a route to finally defining the molecular detail of MT branching at the ultrastructural level.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications of the methodology.

claim: Cleavable affinity purification provides the basis to generate more complex, but molecularly defined, mixes of purified proteins to reconstitute higher-order aspects of spindle formation.
source: More broadly, cleavable affinity purification provides the basis to generate more complex, but molecularly defined, mixes of purified proteins, complete with in vivo PTMs, in order to reconstitute higher-order aspects of spindle formation.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications of the methodology.

claim: By isolating and combining purified, active proteins and protein complexes from any biological system of interest, "cl-AP TRAP" overcomes the limitations of traditional 'bottom-up' approaches.
source: Indeed, by isolating and combining purified, active proteins and protein complexes from any biological system of interest, "cl-AP TRAP" overcomes the limitations of traditional 'bottom-up' approaches, allowing exploration of the level of biological organisation between individual protein and biological process – the level at which emergence of cellular phenomena often occurs.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the significance of their methodology.

claim: Augmin confirms a long-standing hypothesis first articulated to explain the loss of γ-Tubulin on the mitotic spindle when the expression of Augmin subunits is reduced.
source: Our work confirms a long-standing hypothesis, first articulated to explain the loss of γ-Tubulin on the mitotic spindle when the expression of Augmin subunits is reduced (Goshima et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Endogenously expressed, untagged γ-Tubulin is co-purified with γ-Tubulin-GFP at a ratio of ~3:1 γ-Tubulin-GFP: γ-Tubulin.
source: Endogenously expressed, untagged γ-Tubulin is co-purified with γ-Tubulin-GFP, presumably as part of active γ-TuRCs, at a ratio of ~3:1 γ-Tubulin-GFP: γ-Tubulin (as quantified by LiCOR analysis).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Cleavage of proteins from GFP-TRAP-Sulfo-beads reproducibly gave efficiencies of >90%.
source: In contrast, cleavage of proteins and complexes from GFP-TRAP-Sulfo-beads reproducibly gave efficiencies of >90% (n => 10).
evidence: This is stated as a result from multiple experiments.

claim: Cleavage efficiencies from GFP-TRAP-PC beads could not consistently reach greater than 60%.
source: Over the course of the project, different conditions were tried in an attempt to increase the photo-cleaving of GFP, Augmin-GFP and γ-TuRC-GFP from the GFP-TRAP-PC beads. We were unable to consistently reach cleaving efficiencies of greater than 60%.
evidence: This is stated as a result from multiple experiments.

claim: The molar concentration of Augmin purified by cl-AP is 300 nM.
source: Therefore, the number of Augmin complexes in 1 μl of cl-AP supernatant, isolated from GFP-Msd1 expressing embryos, is 1.8 × 1011 and the molar concentration of Augmin is 300 nM.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data as described in Materials and methods.

claim: The molar concentration of γ-TuRC purified by cl-AP is 20 nM.
source: The molar concentration of γ-TuRC purified by cl-AP is therefore 300 nM x 0.6/9 = 20 nM, or the equivalent of 1.8 × 1011×0.6/9 = 1.2×1010 γ-TuRCs per 1 μl.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data as described in Materials and methods.

claim: The final concentration of Augmin in the MT co-sedimentation assay was 60 nM.
source: The final concentration of Augmin in the MT co-sedimentation assay was 60 nM (10 μl in 50 μl total)
evidence: This is stated as the experimental condition.

claim: The final concentration of Augmin in the MT polymerisation assays was 30 nM.
source: while the final concentration of Augmin in the MT polymerisation assays was 30 nM (5 μl in 50 μl total).
evidence: This is stated as the experimental condition.

claim: The final concentration of γ-TuRC in the MT co-sedimentation assay was 4 nM.
source: The final concentration of γ-TuRC in the MT co-sedimentation assay was 4 nM (10 μl in 50 μl total)
evidence: This is stated as the experimental condition.

claim: The final concentration of γ-TuRC in the MT polymerisation assays was 2 nM.
source: while the final concentration of γ-TuRC in the MT polymerisation assays was 2 nM (5 μl in 50 μl total).
evidence: This is stated as the experimental condition.

claim: One γ-TuRC is capable of nucleating 2–3 MTs within 2 mins.
source: Therefore, one γ-TuRC is capable of nucleating 2–3 MTs within 2 mins.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data as described in Materials and methods.

claim: The purified GFP-γ-TuRCs contain 8–10 molecules of GFP-γ-Tubulin (average 9) and 4–5 molecules of unlabelled γ-Tubulin.
source: Therefore, we estimate that the purified GFP-γ-TuRCs contain 8–10 molecules of GFP-γ-Tubulin (average 9) and 4–5 molecules of unlabelled γ-Tubulin.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data as described in Materials and methods.

claim: 60% of the GFP-γ-Tubulin in the purified supernatant is present in fractions consistent with incorporation into γ-TuRCs.
source: Sucrose gradient sedimentation followed by western blotting estimates that 60% of the GFP-γ-Tubulin in the purified supernatant isolated from GFP-γ-Tubulin expressing embryos is present in fractions consistent with incorporation into γ-TuRCs, while 40% is present in fractions consistent with γ-Tubulin that is not part of the γ-TuRC (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sucrose gradient fractionation data in Figure 1f.

claim: 40% of the GFP-γ-Tubulin in the purified supernatant is present in fractions consistent with γ-Tubulin that is not part of the γ-TuRC.
source: Sucrose gradient sedimentation followed by western blotting estimates that 60% of the GFP-γ-Tubulin in the purified supernatant isolated from GFP-γ-Tubulin expressing embryos is present in fractions consistent with incorporation into γ-TuRCs, while 40% is present in fractions consistent with γ-Tubulin that is not part of the γ-TuRC (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sucrose gradient fractionation data in Figure 1f.

claim: 75% of the γ-Tubulin in purified supernatant is present as GFP-γ-Tubulin while 25% is present as γ-Tubulin with no tag.
source: Western blotting of purified supernatant isolated from GFP-γ-Tubulin expressing embryos using anti−γ-Tubulin antibodies estimates that 75% of the γ-Tubulin is present as GFP-γ-Tubulin while 25% is present as γ-Tubulin with no tag (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: An average of 130 MTs were observed per field of view (60.5 μm2) after two mins post-initiation.
source: After two mins post-initiation, an average of 130 MTs were observed per field of view (60.5 μm2) (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantification data in Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: The total number of γ-TuRCs per coverslip is estimated as 6.0 × 10^6.
source: We therefore estimate the total number of γ-TuRCs per coverslip as 6.0 × 106.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data as described in Materials and methods.

claim: There are ~1.32×10^5 fields of view per coverslip.
source: Given there are ~1.32×105 fields of view per coverslip, this equates to 1.7 × 107 MTs per coverslip.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data as described in Materials and methods.

claim: The total number of MTs per coverslip is 1.7 × 10^7.
source: Given there are ~1.32×105 fields of view per coverslip, this equates to 1.7 × 107 MTs per coverslip.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data as described in Materials and methods.

claim: The differences in the time taken for 50% polymerisation between all conditions differs significantly at p=0.001, except when comparing control to Augmin.
source: The differences in the time taken for 50% polymerisation between all conditions differs significantly at p=0.001, except when comparing control to Augmin (ANOVA).
evidence: This is the result of statistical analysis of the polymerization assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient between the length of Augmin-488MTs and the position of γ-TuRC-RhodMT branch points was r = 0.9962 at a p value of < 0.00001.
source: The Pearson correlation coefficient was r = 0.9962 at a p value of < 0.00001.
evidence: This is the result of statistical analysis of the branch position data shown in Figure 3h.

claim: Samples taken at t = 2 and t = 5 min showed similar numbers of MTs to each other, per field of view.
source: Samples taken at t = 2 and t = 5 min showed similar numbers of MTs to each other, per field of view, though the mean length of MTs, and proportion of MTs with branches, were significantly greater after 5 min, than after 2 min (4.01 μm versus 3.24 μm and 34% versus 24%, respectively) (Figure 3b; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data and quantification in Figure 3b and Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: Occasional examples of RhodMTs terminating at 488MTs were observed at a frequency consistent with random placement of MTs on coverslips (~6%).
source: Occasional examples of RhodMTs terminating at 488MTs were observed, but at a frequency consistent with random placement of MTs on coverslips (~6%) (Figure 3b,d; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscopy data and quantification in Figure 3b,d and Figure 3—source data 1.
